caseNote: 가상 사례 (서점용 재고 소프트웨어 회사, 식품 유통사 내부 도구 팀) · 모든 설정은 설명용
insight: 다음 시장은 크기가 아니라 '무엇이 그대로 따라오고 무엇이 새로 바뀌는가'를 세어서 고르고, 고른 뒤에는 강점이 가장 큰 거점부터 들어간다.
misconception: 가장 큰 시장이나 가장 먼저 연락 온 고객이 다음 시장이 되어야 한다. 같은 제품이면 어느 시장이든 비슷하게 팔린다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨 STR-07-02 (핵심과 인접 확장), STR-07-03 (새 시장 진입)
모든 회사, 인원, 고객 수는 설명용 가상 설정

factChecks.note: Ledgerleaf, 고객 400곳, 팀 25명, 유통사 도구 팀 5명은 모두 가상 설정입니다. 실제 기업명과 겹치지 않는지 게시 전에 확인하세요.
6번 카드의 선물 가게 특성(계절성 주문, 위탁 판매)은 '그럴 수 있다(maybe)'는 가정으로만 썼습니다. 일반적 사실로 단정하지 않도록 문구를 유지하세요.
독일 서점 선택지는 언어, 도매상, 지원 시간 차이만 언급했고 특정 국가의 법률·가격 규제는 일부러 다루지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Three emails, one next market
body: Ledgerleaf, a small software company, sells stock and ordering software to about 400 independent bookstores. New sign-ups have slowed.
This week, three emails land. One from a gift shop owner. One from a restaurant group. One from a bookstore in Germany. All three want to buy. The team can only afford to chase one.

image.label: Laptop inbox with three highlighted emails
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 노트북 화면 속 받은편지함에 메일 세 통이 떠 있고 각각 작은 아이콘(선물 상자, 포크와 나이프, 독일어 책 표지 대신 지구본+책)이 붙어 있음. 실제 메일 서비스나 회사 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which market do you go after first?
body: The software tracks stock, suggests reorders and sends orders to book wholesalers. Your team of 25 knows bookstores inside out.
Which email do you answer with a real push?

options.feedback: Gift shops do the same daily job: count stock, reorder, sell over a counter. You change one part, the catalogue, and keep the rest. That's an **adjacent move**.

options.text: Restaurants, the biggest market of the three
options.feedback: The market is big, but the job is different: perishable food, recipes, kitchen staff. You'd change product, customer and sales path at once, which is close to starting a new company.
Same customer and same job, so the product fits. But language, wholesalers, support hours and sales all change. A good move later, once you've learned how to enter a market.

cards.title: Gift shops: same or new?
body: List each part of the business and mark it.

breakdown.label: Daily job
breakdown.detail: Count stock, reorder, sell at a counter

breakdown.label: Where to find them
breakdown.detail: Often on the same shopping streets as your bookstores

breakdown.label: Who buys
breakdown.detail: The owner, usually after a visit in person

breakdown.label: Catalogue
breakdown.detail: No book codes; thousands of small suppliers

cards.callout: Three of four parts carry over. One real gap to fix.

cards.title: Core and adjacent moves
body: Your **core** is the customers, skills and channels you already win with. An **adjacent move** keeps most of the core and changes one part.

Restaurants change almost everything. Germany changes the whole market around the product. Gift shops change one piece, the catalogue. The fewer parts that change, the more of your existing strength comes along.

image.label: Target diagram: core, adjacent ring, far ring
image.brief: 동심원 과녁 인포그래픽. 가운데 "Bookstores (core)", 바로 바깥 고리에 "Gift shops", 같은 고리 반대편에 "Bookstores abroad", 가장 바깥 고리에 "Restaurants". 가운데에서 선물 가게로 짧은 화살표, 레스토랑으로는 긴 점선 화살표.

cards.title: How do you enter the gift shop market?
body: You've picked gift shops. The catalogue gap isn't fixed yet. How do you start?

options.text: Launch nationwide with ads in gift trade magazines
options.feedback: You'd reach many shops fast, but before the gap is fixed. Unhappy early customers in a new market talk, and you learn little that ten shops couldn't teach you.

options.text: Sign 10 gift shops near the bookstores you serve and build the catalogue with them
options.feedback: A foothold, the heart of **entering new markets**: start where your advantage is strongest and learn the differences cheaply. Your bookstore owners can introduce you to their neighbors.

options.text: Create a separate brand and team just for gift shops
options.feedback: Clear focus, but you pay to rebuild sales and support you already have. Keep them shared until the new market proves it needs its own.

cards.title: Ten shops show what a survey misses.
body: Maybe gift shops order big before holidays and little in between. Maybe some stock goods on consignment, paying suppliers only when items sell.
Each surprise is cheap to fix for ten customers. Found after a national launch, it becomes a pile of refunds.
Every market already has its own ways of working. **Entering a new market** means learning them before you scale.

cards.title: Adjacent can quietly split your product.
body: Every gift-shop feature competes with bookstore work for the same 25 people. If bookstore owners see their requests stall, the core starts to leak while you chase the next market.
Set a limit up front, such as a fixed share of engineering time, and keep checking that core customers are staying.
And "adjacent" must be true from the customer's side. If gift shops don't see themselves as similar to bookstores, your pitch won't land.

cards.title: Now you're a team inside a food distributor.
body: You lead a five-person tools team at a regional food distributor. You built a route-planning app the company's delivery drivers love.
Three groups ask for it next. Which do you take on first?

image.label: Delivery truck on a map with three request bubbles
image.brief: 플랫 일러스트. 지도 위 배송 트럭 한 대와 휴대폰 속 경로 앱. 주변에 말풍선 세 개: "Second region drivers", "Warehouse team", "Partner grocery chain". 실제 회사 로고나 상표 없음.

options.text: Drivers in the company's second region
options.feedback: Same users, same job, new roads. Only one part changes, so most of what you built carries over. A classic **adjacent move** and a natural foothold.

options.text: The warehouse team, to plan picking orders
options.feedback: Same building, different job. Picking shelves isn't planning routes, so you'd be building a second product. Possible later, with warehouse staff testing from day one.

options.text: A partner grocery chain that wants to buy it
options.feedback: Selling outside means contracts, pricing and support your team has never done. That's **entering a new market** with almost none of your core in place.

cards.title: Grow where most of your strength comes with you.
body: This lesson used two ideas. **Core and adjacent moves:** count what changes, and prefer the market where only one part does. Entering new markets: start with a foothold where your advantage is strongest, and learn the local ways before you scale.
**Try it today:** write down your next growth idea. List its customers, job, channel and product, and mark each one *same* or *new*.
